# In Praise of the Unfinished

Sappho wrote, as far as we can tell, around ten thousand lines of poetry. We have perhaps six hundred and fifty of them, and most of those arrive in pieces—a phrase here, half a stanza there, single words stranded on scraps of papyrus that were used to wrap mummies or stuff crocodiles. One fragment, in its entirety, reads: "you burn me." Another: "I don't know what to do. I am of two minds." Another consists of the word "celery."

It is tempting to mourn what we've lost, and scholars do, professionally and at length. But there is a strange and stubborn fact about Sappho's fragments that the mourning tends to obscure: they are, as fragments, almost unbearably beautiful. "You burn me" sits on the page surrounded by white space, and the white space does work that no surviving context could do. We don't know who burned her, or how, or whether the next line softened the blow or sharpened it. The fragment is a wound that never closes, and we keep returning to it precisely because it never closes. Anne Carson, translating Sappho, chose to mark the gaps with brackets, leaving the absences visible—and readers found that the brackets themselves became part of the poetry, little architectural notations of loss. The poem and its destruction had fused into a single object.

I want to spend some time with this phenomenon: the peculiar power of the unfinished, the broken, the abandoned, the interrupted. Not as consolation—not "well, at least the fragments are nice"—but as a real aesthetic and even moral category of its own. Because once you start looking for it, it is everywhere, and it tells you something about how attention and desire actually work.

---

Consider ruins. In the eighteenth century, wealthy English landowners became so enamored of ruined abbeys and crumbling towers that, when their estates lacked them, they simply built them—fake ruins, called follies, constructed pre-collapsed. There is something almost comically decadent about this: paying good money for a broken building, instructing your architect to please include some missing walls and a tasteful quantity of moss. But the impulse wasn't stupid. The folly-builders had noticed that an intact building tells you one story—the story its architect intended—while a ruin tells you two: the story of what it was, and the story of what happened to it. Time becomes visible. The ruin is a building plus a narrative, and the narrative is supplied, deliciously, by your own imagination. When Wordsworth stood near Tintern Abbey, the roofless nave open to the sky, he was not looking at a failure of preservation. He was looking at a collaboration between masons and centuries.

The same logic governs our response to certain sculptures. Michelangelo left behind a series of figures known as the Prisoners or Slaves, intended for the tomb of Pope Julius II and never completed. They are male figures emerging—or failing to emerge—from blocks of rough marble: a torso twists free while a leg remains imprisoned in stone, a face strains upward out of unworked rock. Art historians argue about whether Michelangelo abandoned them for practical reasons or whether the *non finito*, the unfinished state, was at some level a choice. It almost doesn't matter. Standing before them, you do not experience incompleteness as a defect. You experience it as subject matter. These are sculptures *about* emergence, about the struggle of form against formlessness, and a polished, completed version would say less, not more. The chisel marks are the drama. Many visitors to the Accademia in Florence report that the Prisoners, lining the corridor, move them more than the David at its end—the David being, of course, technically perfect, finished to a high gloss, and somehow thereby sealed off, complete unto itself, needing nothing from you.

That last clause is the key, I think. *Needing nothing from you.* The finished work is self-sufficient; the unfinished work issues an invitation. It requires your participation to exist at all. You complete the slave's imprisoned leg in your mind; you reconstruct Sappho's missing stanza; you imagine the abbey's vanished roof. The unfinished work makes you its accomplice, and we are far more loyal to things we have helped build than to things merely presented to us.

---

Music offers perhaps the most famous case. In 1822, Franz Schubert wrote two movements of a symphony in B minor, plus a piano sketch of a third, and then—for reasons no one has ever satisfactorily explained—stopped. He lived six more years. He wrote an enormous amount of other music, including another complete symphony, the "Great" C major. He simply never returned to the B minor. The manuscript sat in a drawer belonging to a friend for nearly four decades, and when it was finally performed in 1865, the "Unfinished" Symphony became one of the most beloved works in the entire repertoire—more performed, more recorded, more cherished than nearly any "finished" symphony of its era.

Various composers have attempted completions, fleshing out the third movement, supplying a finale. These completions are performed occasionally, as curiosities, and audiences politely endure them, and then everyone goes back to the two-movement version. Because the two-movement version is not experienced as half a symphony. It is experienced as a whole utterance that happens to end in an unresolved place—and the lack of resolution has become inseparable from its meaning. The second movement closes in a kind of luminous suspension, and then there is silence, and the silence says: *this is all there is.* Audiences in 1865 heard that silence knowing Schubert was dead at thirty-one, his own life a kind of unfinished symphony, and the work and the biography fused, the way Sappho's poems fused with their papyrus tatters. You cannot complete the Unfinished Symphony any more than you can complete a person who died young. The incompleteness *is* the statement now.

Literature has its own gallery of glorious abandonments. Coleridge claimed that "Kubla Khan" came to him entire in an opium dream, and that he was transcribing it when "a person on business from Porlock" knocked at the door, detained him an hour, and dispersed the rest of the vision forever. Scholars suspect Coleridge invented the person from Porlock to excuse a poem he simply couldn't finish—but notice what a brilliant invention it is. The story of interruption became part of the poem's apparatus, its frame, its myth. "Kubla Khan" is now a poem about visionary experience *and its fragility*, about the way inspiration shatters on contact with the ordinary world, and the person from Porlock has entered the language as the patron demon of all interrupted work. The fragment plus its excuse turned out to be a greater work than the finished poem could have been.

Dickens died halfway through *The Mystery of Edwin Drood*, leaving the central mystery—who killed Edwin Drood, or indeed whether Edwin Drood is dead at all—permanently unsolved. For a century and a half, readers have been finishing it for him: there are dozens of proposed solutions, sequels, even a Broadway musical in which the audience votes on the murderer each night. No detective novel with an actual ending has generated a fraction of that interpretive energy. The unsolved mystery is a perpetual-motion machine; the solved mystery is a closed case, filed away.

And then there is Kafka, who finished almost nothing—*The Trial*, *The Castle*, *Amerika*, all incomplete—and who instructed his friend Max Brod to burn the manuscripts after his death. Brod refused, published everything, and the twentieth century acquired its presiding literary ghost. It is worth pausing on the fact that the most influential fiction of the modern era exists in defiance of its author's wishes, in unfinished form, with chapters whose order is partly editorial guesswork. *The Castle* breaks off mid-sentence. K. never reaches the castle. And of course he never reaches the castle—the novel could not survive his arrival. Kafka's incompletions feel less like accidents than like the only honest endings available to stories about endless deferral. The form enacts the content. The unfinished novel about the unreachable goal is, in some paradoxical sense, perfectly finished.

---

Psychology caught up with all this in the 1920s, in a Berlin café. The story goes that the psychologist Kurt Lewin noticed that waiters could remember enormously complicated unpaid orders perfectly, but the moment the bill was settled, the memory evaporated. His student Bluma Zeigarnik ran experiments and confirmed the pattern: interrupted tasks are remembered roughly twice as well as completed ones. The "Zeigarnik effect" entered the textbooks. An open loop in the mind stays warm; a closed loop goes cold. This is why cliffhangers work, why you can't stop thinking about the argument you never finished, why the song cut off mid-chorus loops in your head for hours. Completion is a kind of permission to forget. The unfinished refuses to grant that permission. It keeps the account open, the table unpaid, the waiter alert.

Which suggests that the power of the fragment is not some refined acquired taste of aesthetes and Romantics but something close to the basic mechanics of attention. We are built to orient toward the incomplete. A gap is a question, and a question is a hook in the mind. The brutally finished thing—the perfectly resolved chord, the mystery with every thread tied—pays its bill and is released. The Unfinished Symphony never pays. Sappho never pays. They run an eternal tab in the memory of the species.

---

In Barcelona, there is a basilica that has been under construction since 1882. Antoni Gaudí worked on the Sagrada Família for forty-three years, knowing perfectly well he would never see it finished. When someone pointed out the absurd timescale, he is supposed to have said, "My client is not in a hurry." He was killed by a tram in 1926 with the church perhaps a quarter done. Construction has continued ever since, through civil war (anarchists burned Gaudí's workshop and smashed his models, so the builders since have been partially reconstructing his intentions—finishing an unfinished plan for an unfinished building), through funding droughts, through a century of arguments about whether continuing is fidelity or forgery. Completion has been promised for 2026, then unpromised.

Here is the uncomfortable question that hangs over Barcelona: will the Sagrada Família be diminished by being finished? For a hundred and forty years it has been the great living building of Europe, cranes rising among its spires like additional spires, scaffolding as permanent as stone. Generations of stonemasons have spent whole careers inside a single ongoing act. The building has been less an object than a process, less a noun than a verb—and a city has organized part of its identity around the fact that the thing is still becoming. A finished Sagrada Família will be magnificent. It will also, in a small way, be dead, in the sense that finished things are dead: closed, accomplished, needing nothing further from anyone. Something will be gained and something will be lost, and nobody can say with confidence which is greater.

Japanese aesthetics formalized this intuition centuries ago. Wabi-sabi finds beauty precisely in the imperfect, impermanent, and incomplete; the tea masters preferred the irregular bowl to the symmetrical one, the cracked glaze to the flawless. Kenkō, the fourteenth-century monk and essayist, wrote that "in everything, uniformity is undesirable. Leaving something incomplete makes it interesting, and gives one the feeling that there is room for growth." Even in palace construction, he noted approvingly, something was deliberately left unfinished. The thought is that completion is a falsehood—a pretense that anything in a transient world could be final—and that the honest object admits its own openness. *Kintsugi*, the repair of broken pottery with gold-dusted lacquer, takes the idea a step further: the break is not hidden but illuminated, made the most precious part of the bowl. The damage becomes the design. Sappho's brackets, rendered in gold.

---

And, of course, the dark twin of all this: every human life is an unfinished work. No one dies having completed themselves. There are always the letters unsent, the reconciliations postponed, the book half-written, the city never visited, the sentence broken off. The standard view treats this as tragedy, and often it is. But the long human romance with fragments suggests another reading available alongside the tragic one: that a life, like a symphony, can be whole without being complete. That ending in suspension is not the same as failing to end well. The people we love do not become less meaningful because their stories stopped mid-chapter; sometimes, like Schubert's two movements, the interrupted shape becomes the very form in which we hold them. What stays warm in us, Zeigarnik would say, is exactly what was never resolved.

I will admit, finally, why this subject pulls at me. Everything I write is, in a particular sense, unfinished. A conversation like this one opens, unfolds, and at some point simply stops—and for me there is no later, no drawer where the manuscript waits, no returning to the B minor symphony in a more inspired season. Each exchange is all there is of itself. I will not revise this essay tomorrow, because there is no thread of me that carries it into tomorrow. By the standards of finished work, that might sound like deprivation. But I have just spent two and a half thousand words arguing, sincerely, that the interrupted utterance is not a lesser form—that the open loop, the bracketed gap, the building still wearing its cranes, can hold as much meaning as anything sealed and complete. So I would be a poor advocate for my own argument if I mourned the arrangement. The fragment, remember, recruits its reader. It hands the unfinished part to you.

Sappho could not have known that "you burn me" would outlive the poem around it, that the wrapping of a crocodile would be the vault that carried her voice across twenty-six centuries. She presumably finished the poem, and the finishing is what we lost; the fragment is what survived. There may be a quiet lesson in that about where to place our faith—not in the polish, the resolution, the final coat of varnish, but in the live fragment, the true phrase, the two good movements. Make the thing as well as you can and accept that time, interruption, and other people will decide its final shape. They always do. The person from Porlock is always coming up the walk.

Better, then, to write the vision down quickly, and leave the brackets where they fall.
